analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices and license generic competitors if talks fail.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it sat in House subcommittees until the 115th Congress ended, despite 104 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the government to negotiate drug prices for Medicare's prescription drug benefit instead of paying what manufacturers charge. If a company refused to negotiate a fair price, the government could let other companies make the drug using patents and data the federal government itself granted, paying the original maker reasonable compensation. It would also cap prices at the average of prices in ten wealthy peer countries until a cheaper version arrived.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. Lower negotiated prices would cut out-of-pocket drug costs for seniors and reduce what the government pays through Medicare Part D [S2]. The negotiation factors include patient financial burden and unmet need, not just budget math [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Current law prohibits CMS from negotiating prices under the Medicare drug benefit; the bill would strike that prohibition and require negotiation of prices, discounts, and rebates [S2].

If negotiation fails, the Secretary could authorize competitive licenses letting other manufacturers produce the drug for Medicare despite government-granted exclusivity, with 'reasonable compensation' paid to the original maker [S2].

Until a licensed copy is approved, Medicare plans could pay no more than the average price in ten large OECD countries, and if the maker refused that price, the license would extend to drugs bought by Medicaid, the VA, and the military [S3].
Negotiators must weigh clinical and cost effectiveness, patient financial burden, and unmet patient need, not only the budget [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Medicare and federally funded sales would no longer be set by their monopoly price. Companies that lose could challenge their compensation in the Court of Federal Claims [S3]. Critics of such policies argue weaker exclusivity reduces the reward for developing new drugs, which is the strongest good-faith objection [S2].

drawbacks.text: Overriding market exclusivity, including patents and clinical trial data protections, is an aggressive intervention; drug makers would argue it undercuts the exclusivity incentives that fund new drug development [S3].

The bill leaves the compensation owed to the original maker to the Secretary's judgment across five loosely defined factors, which would likely invite years of litigation in the Court of Federal Claims [S3].
Interim price caps benchmarked to foreign list prices could distort the very prices being averaged, since manufacturers might raise prices abroad to protect the U.S. benchmark [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries and federal taxpayers the upside is large and direct: prices set by negotiation rather than by monopoly, with a foreign price ceiling as a backstop [S2]. The honest cost is the risk to future drug innovation if government-set prices and licensing erode exclusivity incentives, and the likelihood of protracted legal fights over 'reasonable compensation' [S3]. Whether that trade is worth it is a genuine policy judgment, but the bill was never debated in committee, so neither side's arguments were tested in a recorded vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and sent to their health subcommittees, and neither committee ever took it up before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on July 25, 2018, with 104 Democratic cosponsors [S1].
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, then to their health subcommittees within two weeks [S5].
No further action was recorded; no markup, no floor vote, and the Congress ended January 3, 2019 [S5].
All 104 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept their current law protection against Medicare price negotiation, and the Republican House majority avoided a recorded vote on the issue.

sides.party_line_note: All 104 cosponsors were House Democrats and the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority, which held 236 House seats in the 115th Congress [S4].

industries.note: The bill strips their government-granted monopoly pricing in Medicare and could let licensed copies reach any federal program if they refuse foreign-market prices. Their Medicare revenue currently comes from prices set without negotiation, at ordinary beneficiaries' expense.
Competitive licenses would give them a new legal route to manufacture drugs whose patents and data exclusivity were federal grants, with FDA expedited review of their applications.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D insurers
industries.note: Lower negotiated drug prices reduce what plans pay, but the bill lets plans seek discounts below the negotiated price, keeping their bargaining role intact.
